Fireproofing is not there to save the building but to make sure people can evacuate before the building collapses; when the code says all office buildings need a two-hour fire rating it means two hours to evacuate. On 9/23 she repeated that steel exposed to high temperatures loses its strength and becomes ribbon candy, adding that she imagines it probably does melt too. (This entry stores her version only.)
answers: What is the fire danger to steel, and what does a two-hour fire rating mean?

term: Why the hole is the bolt diameter plus 1/8 in (1/16 + 1/16)
her_words: Tension in the bolt hole is actually the bolt diameter plus an eighth of an inch. Why? It's manufactured to be a 16th inch of a diameter.
We also subject an additional 16 th of an inch because the process for making these holes can damage the materials.
The hole is an eighth of an inch larger. 16th of an inch because the process of making the bolt hold the material.

The area taken out is a rectangle: this full hole width times the thickness of the element. She repeated the 1/8 in rule among the midterm topics on 9/30 and said she still wants the class to understand how bolts work.
answers: Why is the hole bolt diameter + 1/8 in?

term: Why the live-load factor 1.6 is bigger than the dead-load factor 1.2
her_words: Live load is harder to grasp. It was an apartment now a fraternity. Have parties every night.
We can be very accurate with dead load and less accurate with live loads. So that's a bigger safety factor.
summary: She can estimate dead load pretty accurately if the architect and the designs are good; live load is harder to grasp (an apartment that becomes a fraternity with parties every night; 50-year storms). So the live load needs the bigger safety factor: 1.2 on dead load and 1.6 on live load. Putting one safety factor on the material side says the two loads are equally uncertain, which she said is not what we feel today: we can be very accurate with dead load and less accurate with live loads.
answers: Why is the live-load factor larger than the dead-load factor?
Why compare load combinations instead of one factor on the material side?

term: Strain is how much a member stretches: the change in length, designated epsilon
her_words: Tension forces. It's going to want to grow a little bit.
Strain: Is it equal to the change in length, designated epsilon?
Applied forces -> Physical change (change in length or shape)
Steel subject to an applied Tension Force P will elongate Delta
summary: When you put a load on a structure there is a physical change: in tension it is going to want to grow a little bit (stretch). That physical response is strain, the change in length (relative to the original length, delta over L), designated epsilon. Her week-1 slide: applied forces give a physical change (change in length or shape); steel under a tension force P will elongate by delta, and strain is epsilon = delta / L, plotted against stress f = P/A. She pictured it in tension because it is easier to visualize.
answers: What is strain, and which Greek letter stands for it?
What is the physical response of a member to a load?

Short Columns fail by crushing
summary: Short columns crush: the maximum load the material can resist is exceeded, the strength of the steel is exhausted and the column squashes (her slide calls it an inelastic failure: material strength is exhausted). Long columns do not crush; they buckle.
answers: How does a short column fail?
What is crushing in a compression member?

her_words: And if it becomes geometrically unstable, it buckles.
Long columns fail and buckle. They become unstable about the weaker of two axis.
It'll buckle first about the axis with the smaller r.
summary: If a compression member becomes geometrically unstable it buckles: long columns buckle, becoming unstable about the weaker of the two axes, and elastic buckling happens well before the strength of the steel is exhausted. A column starts to deform (curve), and it buckles first about the axis with the smaller r, the more 'spaghetti-like' (more slender) direction.
answers: How does a long column fail?
About which axis does a column buckle first?

it fails abruptly because it's brittle
summary: Her slides: steel is ductile, it withstands large deformations without failure (the plastic range gives local deformations before failure and lets stresses be redistributed), against a brittle material such as concrete, which fails suddenly.
